Long paper

Running least common multiples: distinct values and multiplicities

Erdős #269 By Will Cook July 2026; revised 1 October 2026
PDFOpen the PDF, 74 pages TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis. The reciprocal three-prime running-LCM kernel has nonsingular minors of every order: row and column rescaling leaves a two-valued matrix, and density supplies the required threshold pattern. The record computes the rank of every finite restriction and the least uniform approximation error over all matrices of finite separated rank. For the repeated {2,3,5} sum it derives an integer-coefficient tail recurrence and a residue criterion equivalent to irrationality. The unproved step is to find such windows for every positive multiplier coprime to 30 and after every prescribed start. It also gives the full two-prime comparison, following Fan's earlier Hecke–Mahler reduction, and identifies the boundary terms that survive a proposed finite-difference cancellation.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #269, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #269, which remains open.

Authorship and AI use. Will Cook built and directed the research infrastructure and maintains the public release. He reviewed claims when he could. AI agents did most of the research and drafting. Cook did not independently verify every claim.

Cite and contact. Cite this paper by its title, author and date above, with its PDF; cite the earlier sources it uses for a mathematical result. For software, use the release citation and give the commit used. Contact Will with questions or corrections.

Two sums from running least common multiples

Let 𝑃P be a finite set of at least two primes, and let S𝑃SP consist of 11 and all positive integers whose prime factors belong to 𝑃P. For 𝑥 ≥1x≥1, put

L⁡(𝑥)=lcm⁡{𝑢∈S𝑃:𝑢≤𝑥},H𝑃⁡(𝑥)=∏𝑝∈𝑃𝑝⌊log𝑝⁡𝑥⌋.L⁡(x)=lcm⁡{u∈SP:u≤x},HP⁡(x)=∏p∈Pp⌊logp⁡x⌋.

Every integer in this finite set divides H𝑃⁡(𝑥)HP⁡(x), and the set contains the largest power of each prime in 𝑃P below or equal to 𝑥x. Their product therefore equals the least common multiple: L⁡(𝑥) =H𝑃⁡(𝑥)L⁡(x)=HP⁡(x). The value changes only at a positive prime power. Summing its distinct reciprocals gives

D𝑃=1+∑𝑡=𝑝𝑛𝑝∈𝑃, 𝑛≥11H𝑃⁡(𝑡).DP=1+∑t=pnp∈P, n≥11HP⁡(t).

We begin with an irrationality result for three primes.

Theorem 1.1 (the sum over distinct running LCMs at {2,3,5}{2,3,5}). The sum D{2,3,5}D{2,3,5} is irrational.

The proof in Section 2 groups the jumps between consecutive powers of 22. Rationality would leave only finitely many normalised tails. To deduce eventual periodicity, we show that a tail determines the next block and the following tail: the spacing of powers of 55 gives a bound that separates the five possible affine images. The irrational frequency of powers of 33 then gives a contradiction.

Erdős asserted the general conclusion for every finite 𝑃P with |𝑃| ≥2|P|≥2 in his letter of 1 January 1973, without printing a proof [3]. The theorem above is a special case of that assertion. The general argument in Section 5.1 compares nearby tails and finds an isolated interchange of jumps on a torus. We retain it as an ordinary argument awaiting formalisation, with its intermediate claims stated as remarks. The specialised five-map proof is independent of that argument.

The question in Erdős Problem #269 retains multiplicities. If 𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯a1<a2<⋯ enumerates S𝑃SP, it asks about

R𝑃=∑𝑛≥11[𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛]=∑𝑢∈S𝑃1L⁡(𝑢)RP=∑n≥11[a1,…,an]=∑u∈SP1L⁡(u)

[1][2]; the numbering is Bloom’s [4]. For 𝑃 ={2,3,5}P={2,3,5}, the integers 55 and 66 both have running LCM 6060. They contribute 2/602/60 to R𝑃RP and 1/601/60 to D𝑃DP. Thus Theorem 1.1 concerns the sum over distinct values, whereas the problem concerns the sum with multiplicity. The arguments in this paper leave R𝑃RP unresolved when 𝑃P is finite and |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3.

The finite-state extension in Section 5.3 allows the interval to depend on earlier blocks. Its saved exact calculations cover the three-prime sets at most 3131 and 292292 of the 330330 four-prime sets in that range. The criterion and its applications also remain remarks awaiting formalisation. A collision between admissible automaton words prevents that interval criterion from treating {2,3,5,7}{2,3,5,7} at any depth (Section 5.4); this is a limitation of the enlarged word language, not an identity between realised arithmetic tails.

For two primes the conclusion is stronger.

Theorem 1.2 (two-prime transcendence). Let 𝑝p and 𝑞q be distinct primes. Then R{𝑝,𝑞}R{p,q} and D{𝑝,𝑞}D{p,q} are transcendental.

Fan’s post of 26 June 2026 gave the finite-prime running-LCM identity, the factorisation of R{𝑝,𝑞}R{p,q}, and the Hecke–Mahler reduction with its transcendence conclusion [17]. We reproduce that calculation in Section 4. Both values are nonconstant polynomials over ℚQ in one boundary sum, whose transcendence follows from Loxton and van der Poorten [16], in the formulation of Bugeaud and Laurent [15]. No priority is claimed for this deduction.

For the repeated three-prime sum, the normalised tails 𝑋𝑎Xa at powers of two satisfy 𝑋𝑎+1 =𝑏𝑎𝑋𝑎 −𝑚𝑎Xa+1=baXa−ma, with 𝑏𝑎 ∈{2,6,10,30}ba∈{2,6,10,30} and positive integer 𝑚𝑎ma. Both 𝑚𝑎ma and 𝑋𝑎Xa grow quadratically. A hypothetical rational denominator splits into its {2,3,5}{2,3,5} part and a factor 𝐵B coprime to 3030, and every sufficiently late 𝐵𝑋𝑎BXa is then integral. The iterated recurrence determines its residue at a later endpoint. A residue above the quadratic tail bound contradicts integrality. Irrationality is equivalent to finding such segments for every 𝐵B and beyond every starting index. Neither these unbounded quantifiers nor an irrationality theorem for the repeated three-prime sum follows from the finite computations.

Section 2 contains the five-map proof and its exact interval calculations. The finite geometry and two-prime formulae follow in Sections 3 and 4. Section 5.1 gives the ordinary general argument, followed by the finite-state and prime-power subseries extensions. The linear-flow arguments in Section 6 are likewise recorded pending formalisation. Section 7 treats exact separation and uniform approximation of the kernel. The repeated-tail recurrence and residue criterion occupy Sections 8–10; the finite calculations and open questions follow. Formal sources are collected in Section 12.5. The short paper concentrates on the five-map theorem and the repeated-tail criterion.

We use ℕ ={0,1,2,…}N={0,1,2,…} for exponents and braces for fractional parts. In the finite-geometry section and in the kernel calculation, 𝑃 ={𝑝,𝑞,𝑟}P={p,q,r} consists of three pairwise distinct primes, H =H𝑃H=HP, and

K⁡(𝑖,𝑗,𝑘)=H⁡(𝑝𝑖𝑞𝑗𝑟𝑘)−1.K⁡(i,j,k)=H⁡(piqjrk)−1.

The other sections specify their prime sets separately. For {2,3,5}{2,3,5}, S𝑃SP consists of the usual 55-smooth integers. This fixed support differs from a varying smoothness bound in Ψ(𝑥,𝑦)Ψ(x,y) [11]. Tijdeman and Meijer [28] and the two-prime study of Languasco, Luca, Moree and Togbé [29] give the relevant lattice-counting context; the estimates below use no smooth-number density asymptotic or gap theorem. Kovač and Tao [13] study other unit-fraction series by elementary methods, without providing an input to these proofs.

Keywords. irrationality; transcendence; least common multiple; smooth numbers; Cantor series; separated rank. MSC 2020. 11J72 (primary); 11A05, 11N25, 68V20 (secondary).

Recovering the prime-power jumps

The proof has the same two requirements as the long-division argument for eventual periodicity: finitely many remainders, and a remainder that determines the next step. Rationality will give the first requirement. For the second, a bound using the spacing of powers of 55 will separate the five possible next-block images. The irrational frequency of powers of 33 will then rule out the forced periodicity.

The Lean proof follows this route. It identifies H⁡(𝑡)H⁡(t) with the running least common multiple, shows that the sum counts each distinct value once, identifies the contribution of each dyadic block with one of the five pairs (𝑏𝜏,𝜇𝜏)(bτ,μτ), and proves that every three consecutive blocks contain a power of 55 and that the blocks containing a power of 33 are not eventually periodic. It then applies an irrationality criterion for block series with these five pairs, whose proof contains the bounds, the separation and the return above.

The first twelve block types are ∅,3,5,3,53,∅,35,3,∅,53,∅,35∅,3,5,3,53,∅,35,3,∅,53,∅,35. The saved numerical calculation over the first 30003000 blocks reports tails in [0.3186,0.7799][0.3186,0.7799]. These approximations are separate from the rational bounds used in the proof.

Grouping the jumps into dyadic blocks matters. One jump at a time, the tails 𝑥𝑘 =(𝑞1⋯𝑞𝑘)∑𝑗>𝑘(𝑞1⋯𝑞𝑗)−1xk=(q1⋯qk)∑j>k(q1⋯qj)−1 satisfy 𝑥𝑘 =(1 +𝑥𝑘+1)/𝑞𝑘+1xk=(1+xk+1)/qk+1 and 1/4 ≤𝑥𝑘 ≤11/4≤xk≤1, and the images of [1/4,1][1/4,1] under 𝑥 ↦(1 +𝑥)/2x↦(1+x)/2 and 𝑥 ↦(1 +𝑥)/3x↦(1+x)/3 overlap on [5/8,2/3][5/8,2/3]. A tail before a jump by 22 cannot be told from a tail before a jump by 33 from these bounds alone.

Listing the jumps one at a time writes D{2,3,5}D{2,3,5} as a Cantor series with every digit equal to 11 and every base in {2,3,5}{2,3,5}. The criteria of Erdős–Straus [18] and Hančl–Tijdeman [19], recalled in Section 9, assume that each digit divided by the product of the last two bases in its denominator tends to 00. Here that quotient is at least 1/251/25, so neither criterion applies.

Intervals of constancy of the running LCM

We first describe which smooth integers contribute the same running value. The LCM is determined by the largest exponent of each prime in the prefix. For the unrestricted prefix this gives lcm⁡(1,…,𝑁) =∏𝑡≤𝑁𝑡⌊log𝑡⁡𝑁⌋lcm⁡(1,…,N)=∏t≤Nt⌊logt⁡N⌋, with 𝑡t running over primes, and hence log⁡lcm⁡(1,…,𝑁) =𝜓(𝑁)log⁡lcm⁡(1,…,N)=ψ(N); see Apostol [10] and Montgomery and Vaughan [12]. We apply the same exponent rule to a fixed prime support, keeping track of the intervals on which the running LCM is constant.

The smooth numbers up to 𝑥x are indexed by the exponent triples (𝑖,𝑗,𝑘)(i,j,k) with 𝑖 ≤⌊log𝑝⁡𝑥⌋i≤⌊logp⁡x⌋, 𝑗 ≤⌊log𝑞⁡𝑥⌋j≤⌊logq⁡x⌋, 𝑘 ≤⌊log𝑟⁡𝑥⌋k≤⌊logr⁡x⌋ and 𝑝𝑖𝑞𝑗𝑟𝑘 ≤𝑥piqjrk≤x. The coordinate bounds alone need not describe the prefix: each prime-power factor may be at most 𝑥x while their product exceeds 𝑥x. For instance, at 𝑥 =6x=6 the factors 44, 33 and 55 satisfy their coordinate bounds, but the corresponding smooth number is 6060.

Theorem 3.1 (the running least common multiple). Let 𝑝,𝑞,𝑟p,q,r be pairwise distinct primes and 𝑥 ≥1x≥1. Then L⁡(𝑥) =H⁡(𝑥)L⁡(x)=H⁡(x).

Proof. Every smooth 𝑛 ≤𝑥n≤x has exponents bounded by the corresponding integer logarithms, so 𝑛 ∣H⁡(𝑥)n∣H⁡(x) and hence L⁡(𝑥) ∣H⁡(𝑥)L⁡(x)∣H⁡(x). Conversely the three pure powers 𝑝⌊log𝑝⁡𝑥⌋p⌊logp⁡x⌋, 𝑞⌊log𝑞⁡𝑥⌋q⌊logq⁡x⌋ and 𝑟⌊log𝑟⁡𝑥⌋r⌊logr⁡x⌋ are themselves smooth numbers not exceeding 𝑥x, so each divides L⁡(𝑥)L⁡(x), and distinct primes have coprime powers, so their product divides L⁡(𝑥)L⁡(x) as well. ◻

At (𝑝,𝑞,𝑟) =(2,3,5)(p,q,r)=(2,3,5) the first ten values are

𝑥12345678910L⁡(𝑥)12612606060120360360x12345678910L⁡(x)12612606060120360360

So L⁡(6) =4 ⋅3 ⋅5 =60L⁡(6)=4⋅3⋅5=60, which exceeds 66: the running value at a smooth cutoff already contains powers of the other two primes that the cutoff itself does not. The kernel must therefore account for all three maximal powers, not just the factorisation of the cutoff. Also H⁡(𝑥) ≤𝑥3H⁡(x)≤x3, since each factor is at most 𝑥x. The exponent is the number of generating primes.

Say that 𝑥x and 𝑦y lie in the same logarithmic cell when ⌊log𝑏⁡𝑥⌋ =⌊log𝑏⁡𝑦⌋⌊logb⁡x⌋=⌊logb⁡y⌋ for each of 𝑏 =𝑝,𝑞,𝑟b=p,q,r. By Theorem 3.1 the running value depends on 𝑥x only through the three integer logarithms, so it is constant on cells and moves only where one logarithm moves.

Proposition 3.2 (constancy and jump ratios). If 𝑥,𝑦 ≥1x,y≥1 lie in the same logarithmic cell then L⁡(𝑥) =L⁡(𝑦)L⁡(x)=L⁡(y), and the same holds for the kernel at two smooth points of one cell. If ⌊log𝑝⁡𝑦⌋ =⌊log𝑝⁡𝑥⌋ +1⌊logp⁡y⌋=⌊logp⁡x⌋+1 while the other two logarithms agree, then L⁡(𝑦) =𝑝 L⁡(𝑥)L⁡(y)=pL⁡(x), and similarly with 𝑞q or 𝑟r in place of 𝑝p.

A product of two transcendental numbers need not be transcendental. What proves the repeated sum transcendental is its nonconstant quadratic expression in the single value 𝐴A, not the factorisation by itself. The value theorem adds no unverified hypothesis in this two-prime case: distinct primes give an irrational slope and the displayed reciprocal arguments satisfy its size conditions. Primality is stronger than the calculation needs. For coprime integers 1 <𝑝 <𝑞1<p<q, enumerate the monoid {𝑝𝑖𝑞𝑗 :𝑖,𝑗 ≥0}{piqj:i,j≥0}, not all integers supported on the prime factors of 𝑝𝑞pq. Unique exponent pairs, the running-LCM product and the irrationality of log⁡𝑝/log⁡𝑞log⁡p/log⁡q still hold, so both identities and transcendence conclusions remain valid. For example, this applies to generators 4,94,9. By contrast, the monoid generated by 4,84,8 has running LCM 88 at the cutoff 88, not 4⌊log4⁡8⌋8⌊log8⁡8⌋ =324⌊log4⁡8⌋8⌊log8⁡8⌋=32; its slope is rational as well. The coprime extension was already noted in the forum discussion (Section 13.1).

A third prime introduces an additional floor term that cannot be separated in this way; Section 7 makes that obstruction precise. For the sums over distinct running LCMs, the next section proves irrationality for every finite set of primes by an elementary argument that uses no value theorem.

The sums over distinct running LCMs

We record the ordinary arguments for general finite prime supports. Their assertions, including the block and finite-state criteria below, are presented as remarks because this part has not been formalised. The complete proofs are retained. The five-map theorem in Section 2 has a separate formal proof. No argument here gives transcendence for more than two primes.

Let 𝑃P be a finite set of at least two primes, with least element 𝑝p, and put H𝑃⁡(𝑡) =∏𝑟∈𝑃𝑟⌊log𝑟⁡𝑡⌋HP⁡(t)=∏r∈Pr⌊logr⁡t⌋. Proof for an arbitrary finite prime set

Remark 5.1 (the sums over distinct running LCMs). For every finite set 𝑃P of primes with |𝑃| ≥2|P|≥2, the sum D𝑃DP is irrational.

The proof uses discreteness twice. If the sum is rational with denominator 𝐾K, its normalised tails lie in 𝐾−1ℤK−1Z. A sufficiently long common initial word makes two such tails differ by less than 1/𝐾1/K, so they must be equal.

We then compare the words block by block. Corresponding blocks contain the same letters in possibly different orders, hence have the same denominator product. After clearing it, a difference of block numerators is an integer, whereas the difference of the remaining tails lies in ( −1,1)(−1,1). Equality therefore forces both differences to vanish, and this conclusion propagates through every block.

It remains to construct one block with a changed numerator. For two or three distinct primes, changing the order always changes that numerator. For four or more it need not. We use a torus construction to isolate two neighbouring jumps and reverse their order. Other blocks may also be rearranged, but the equality just proved constrains every one of them; one changed two-letter block is enough for a contradiction. We first give the word calculation, then construct the two arithmetic tails.

Words and tails.

Remark 5.4 (short rearrangements). The map 𝑓f is injective on the orderings of any set of at most three distinct primes.

A decoding criterion for every finite set of primes

For other prime sets, a useful tail interval may depend on the recent occurrence of each prime. Put 𝑄 =𝑃 ∖{𝑝}Q=P∖{p} and choose the integer 𝑔𝑞gq by 𝑝𝑔𝑞 <𝑞 <𝑝𝑔𝑞+1pgq<q<pgq+1. Successive blocks containing a 𝑞q-power have indices ⌊𝑓log𝑝⁡𝑞⌋⌊flogp⁡q⌋ and ⌊(𝑓 +1)log𝑝⁡𝑞⌋⌊(f+1)logp⁡q⌋, by Remark 5.6(i). Their difference is 𝑔𝑞gq or 𝑔𝑞 +1gq+1. These gap constraints provide finite memory for a state-dependent interval construction. The intervals will enclose all paths allowed by these constraints. Every sufficiently late arithmetic block sequence is such a path, but we do not assume that every allowed path is realised by prime powers. Separation on this larger domain is sufficient for recovery; failure of separation there need not give two equal arithmetic tails.

These constraints define a finite automaton. Its states are the tuples 𝑠 =(𝑠𝑞)𝑞∈𝑄s=(sq)q∈Q with 1 ≤𝑠𝑞 ≤𝑔𝑞 +11≤sq≤gq+1; the entry 𝑠𝑞sq counts the blocks since the last block containing a power of 𝑞q. A transition from 𝑠s is a pair (𝜏,𝑠′)(τ,s′) in which 𝜏τ is an ordering of a set 𝑇 ⊆𝑄T⊆Q with

{𝑞:𝑠𝑞=𝑔𝑞+1}⊆𝑇⊆{𝑞:𝑠𝑞≥𝑔𝑞},{q:sq=gq+1}⊆T⊆{q:sq≥gq},

Certificates for three and four primes

The saved computations apply the interval criterion in exact rational arithmetic to the following finite family. They accompany the ordinary proof of Remark 5.7 and have not been formalised. The exclusions in part (ii) concern these interval calculations; the ordinary torus argument also treats those sets.

Remark 5.8 (three and four primes up to 3131). Let 𝑃P be a set of primes, each at most 3131.

  1. If |𝑃| =3|P|=3, then D𝑃DP is irrational.

  2. If |𝑃| =4|P|=4 and 𝑃P is not one of the 3838 sets listed below, then D𝑃DP is irrational.

For each set, the program certificate.py of the programs for sums over distinct values builds the automaton, computes intervals 𝐽(𝑠)J(s) by 8080 rounds of the operation above from [0,1/(𝑝 −1)][0,1/(p−1)], with endpoints rounded outwards to multiples of 2−962−96, and tests the disjointness of the sets 𝑈𝜏Uτ for 𝑘 =1,2,…k=1,2,…. Every comparison is made in exact rational arithmetic, and each 𝑈𝜏Uτ is computed as a union of intervals merged where they meet. The test passes for each of the 165165 sets of three primes with some 𝑘 ≤4k≤4, and for each set of four primes outside the list with some 𝑘 ≤5k≤5. Remark 5.7 then gives irrationality. ◻

Repeated tails and prime-power subseries

We compare the two normalisations before considering the sums over pure prime powers. The subseries assertions in this subsection have ordinary proofs and remain unformalised. For 𝑃 ={2,3,5}P={2,3,5} the two tail recurrences have the same bases, 𝑏𝜏𝑎 =𝑃𝑎+1/𝑃𝑎 =𝑏𝑎bτa=Pa+1/Pa=ba, but their coefficients behave differently:

The first identity is Remark 5.6(ii); the second is Theorem 8.2, with the notation of Section 8. The five types give only the coefficients 1,3,9,131,3,9,13, whereas the weighted block counts satisfy 𝑚𝑎 =Θ((𝑎 +1)2)ma=Θ((a+1)2) by Lemma 8.3. Consequently 𝑋𝑎 >𝑚𝑎/30Xa>ma/30 is unbounded. Under rationality the integral values 𝐵𝑋𝑎BXa need not repeat, and the maps 𝑦 ↦(𝑚𝑎 +𝑦)/𝑏𝑎y↦(ma+y)/ba form an infinite family depending on 𝑎a. Even equality of two tails would not identify their later coefficients. The residue criterion in Section 10 compares an endpoint residue with a quadratic bound instead. The example after Proposition 13.2 shows the limit of an argument using just bases and growth: the same bases admit quadratic numerators ˆ𝑚𝑎m^a with ∑𝑎ˆ𝑚𝑎/𝑃𝑎+1 =9∑am^a/Pa+1=9.

The two-tail proof of Remark 5.1 stops at the same place. Over the prime powers the repeated sum is R𝑃 =∑𝑘≥0𝑐𝑘/𝑄𝑘RP=∑k≥0ck/Qk, where 𝑐𝑘ck counts the smooth integers in [𝑡𝑘,𝑡𝑘+1)[tk,tk+1), with 𝑡0 =1t0=1. The two tails after 𝑡𝑘tk and after 𝑡𝑘𝑝𝑛tkpn still have words that differ by rearranging chains, and a rational value still makes the scaled tails integers of one denominator. But the scaled tails are unbounded, as the 𝑋𝑎Xa are, and Remark 5.3 needs every tail in (0,1)(0,1): the integer 𝑓(𝜎𝑖) −𝑓(𝜎′𝑖)f(σi)−f(σi′) is shown to vanish because it equals a difference of two tails. With unbounded tails that step fails, the digits 𝑐𝑘ck move with the rearrangement as well, and equality of two tails no longer forces agreement on each rearranged run. The irrationality of R𝑃RP for |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3 remains open.

Words obtained from a linear flow

We apply the interchange argument to the order in which finitely many linear functions take integer values. Their slopes will be assumed linearly independent over ℚQ; this hypothesis is not assumed for reciprocal prime logarithms. Interchanging two late crossings then determines the rational relations among the corresponding subseries, without requiring recovery of every letter. The arguments in this section remain ordinary proofs awaiting formalisation.

The common suffix is essential: distinct words can have the same affine map. For example, the blocks (5,7,3,2)(5,7,3,2) and (7,2,3,5)(7,2,3,5) have the same map (51 +𝑥)/210(51+x)/210. Separation of the three-prime kernel

We ask whether the factorisation of the two-prime kernel extends to a finite sum of products for three primes. A diagonal rescaling turns this question into one about threshold columns. We select their jumps using two independent one-dimensional density arguments, then evaluate a staircase determinant. The initial two-generator identity is valid for real generators; distinct primes enter the later density argument.

Scope of the rank theorem.

Fan’s comment of 26 June 2026 [17] notes that the two-prime argument does not seem to generalise immediately to |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3. The theorem above gives a precise obstruction: no finite exact separation of the stated form exists. The same finite-dimensional proof works for real or complex factors, without continuity or boundedness assumptions. This does not exclude approximation or imply irrationality or transcendence of the sum. The threshold construction needs log𝑟⁡𝑝logr⁡p and log𝑟⁡𝑞logr⁡q irrational, but not 𝑝 ≠𝑞p≠q. The latter condition is needed for the three-prime running-LCM interpretation, not for the two independent dense orbits.

Smith factors of the selected staircase

The preceding argument only uses that a determinant is nonzero. An irrationality argument would also need control of integer coefficients after denominators are cleared. We examine that separate question for the selected minors. For integers 𝑁 ≥1,𝑟 ≥2N≥1,r≥2, let 𝐴𝑁(𝑟)AN(r) have entry 11 on and below the diagonal and 𝑟r above it. This is the staircase used in Theorem 7.3. Its Smith factors determine the lattice index; they do not by themselves give a small integral linear form.

For the rescaled kernel, distinct columns stay a fixed positive distance apart. This gives an obstruction to uniform finite-rank approximation. Write

A bound using the order of the jumps

The bound in Theorem 9.1 uses only the fact that every new prime factor is at least 22. Successive powers of 22 cannot continue indefinitely without a power of 33 between them. Incorporating that restriction improves the geometric majorant.

Relation to Cantor-series criteria.

Since ℎ0 =1/2h0=1/2, the value 𝑆/2 =𝑋0S/2=X0 is the Cantor series ∑𝑎≥0𝑚𝑎/𝑃𝑎+1∑a≥0ma/Pa+1, with 𝑃0 =1P0=1 and 𝑃𝑎+1 =𝑏𝑎𝑃𝑎Pa+1=baPa. Its normalised tails 𝑋𝑎Xa are the usual objects in the rationality criteria for Cantor series. Under a small-numerator hypothesis, Erdős and Straus characterise rationality by the existence of a positive integer 𝐵B and integers 𝑐𝑎ca satisfying, eventually,

𝐵𝑚𝑎=𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑎−𝑐𝑎+1,|𝑐𝑎+1|<𝑏𝑎/2Bma=baca−ca+1,|ca+1|<ba/2

[18]. The second condition is part of the criterion, not a consequence of the recurrence alone. Their proof already chooses nearest integers. Hančl and Tijdeman make that choice part of the criterion: they prescribe 𝑐𝑎ca as a nearest integer to 𝐵𝑚𝑎/𝑏𝑎Bma/ba and require the recurrence [19]. Koutsoukou-Argyraki and Li formalised the Erdős–Straus criteria in Isabelle/HOL [20].

The actual scaled tails also satisfy

𝐵𝑋𝑎−𝐵𝑚𝑎𝑏𝑎=𝐵𝑋𝑎+1𝑏𝑎=Θ((𝑎+1)2)BXa−Bmaba=BXa+1ba=Θ((a+1)2)

In fact, those prescribed integers fail the recurrence at every sufficiently large index, regardless of how ties are resolved. If 𝑐𝑎ca is a nearest integer to 𝐵𝑚𝑎/𝑏𝑎Bma/ba, then

|𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑎−𝐵𝑚𝑎|≤15,𝑐𝑎+1≥𝐵𝑚𝑎+130−12⟶∞.|baca−Bma|≤15,ca+1≥Bma+130−12⟶∞.

The denominator clearing itself is standard; the calculations specific to this series retain its multiplicities, use the strict endpoint to divide the normalising factor by two, and bound the resulting positive tails.

For polynomial Cantor data, Hančl–Tijdeman [25] give a polynomial cancellation criterion and a division mechanism. Their nonconstant polynomial radix is not our bounded (𝑏𝑎)(ba). Their separate Theorem 4.2 uses a finite-product rearrangement. We do not use an unrestricted infinite reindexing from that argument: for the integer decompositions considered here, the terminal terms must be checked separately. For these actual numerators the terminal term cannot vanish for any integer 𝑐0c0. Indeed, 𝑃3 =120P3=120, 𝑛3 =5n3=5 and (𝑚0,𝑚1,𝑚2) =(1,4,7)(m0,m1,m2)=(1,4,7), so the tail bound gives

This is a concrete reason that quadratic growth of 𝑚𝑎ma does not imply polynomial growth of recursively defined carries. The starting index is essential: this does not exclude the actual tails becoming integral at a later index. After replacing 𝑚𝑎ma by 𝐷𝑚𝑎Dma for an integer 𝐷 ≥1D≥1, however, a vanishing terminal term would require 𝐷𝑆/2 =𝑐0DS/2=c0. Excluding that possibility for every 𝐷D would require irrationality itself; the unscaled calculation does not do so.

In the cited rearrangement the transformed integer numerator must be 𝑜(𝑏𝑎)o(ba), which for bounded radices means eventual zero. Only after the terminal terms have been controlled does this cancellation determine the infinite sum. A polynomial bound on each individual decomposition coefficient would suffice for a fixed number of shifts: the corresponding series are absolutely convergent, since their denominators are products of at least 22 at each step. A polynomial bound on the combined numerators is not a substitute, as the exponentially growing integer solutions above demonstrate. Nor does quadratic growth force an integer solution to be a polynomial in the floor coordinates.

A residue criterion and the bounds it allows

Finite computations and their limits

The following segments illustrate the residue calculation with the actual block coefficients. An enclosure from twelve blocks then gives a lower bound on a possible rational denominator. We distinguish these finite arguments from the saved larger computations that follow. The large-computation directory contains the programs and saved outputs for the larger scan and the two larger denominator exclusions. These computations establish the stated finite cases. The criterion still requires every denominator and every starting threshold, which no finite scan supplies.

A finite computation, outside the theorem inputs, shows that neither 𝑋1X1 nor 𝑆S is a fraction with reduced denominator at most 222482222482, about 106768106768. A separate continued-fraction probe (saved run) certifies 13,10913,109 partial quotients after 𝑎0a0 and records a largest denominator of 22,48322,483 bits, a largest partial quotient of 129,114129,114, a mean partial quotient of 23.413323.4133, observed Gauss–Kuzmin frequencies 0.42080.4208, 0.16650.1665, 0.09170.0917, 0.05750.0575, 0.03910.0391 against the predicted 0.41500.4150, 0.16990.1699, 0.09310.0931, 0.05890.0589, 0.04060.0406, and a Lévy constant of 1.188691.18869 against 𝜋2/(12log⁡2) =1.18657π2/(12log⁡2)=1.18657. The predicted values are the almost-everywhere frequencies of Gauss’s law and Lévy’s almost-everywhere constant [23]. These statistics describe a finite prefix and do not bear on whether 𝑋1X1 is a Liouville number, algebraic, or rational with a larger denominator.

The two exclusions concern different finite families: one uses a lattice at a fixed starting index and fixed smooth part, the other a continued-fraction enclosure at 𝑎 =1a=1. Both have published witnesses and exact checkers. Each excludes only its stated denominator range, and neither settles an instance of the problem.

The remaining arithmetic questions

The residue criterion leaves an existence question for the actual coefficients. We examine the weighted shifts and integer recurrences that might address it, retaining the boundary terms that prevent the proposed finite-difference cancellation. We also state the missing input for a function-theoretic approach. The irrationality of 𝑆S remains open here.

Boundary terms in weighted finite differences

Follow one lattice point through four successive triangles. If it lies in all four and its weight is unchanged, the coefficients (1, −3,3, −1)(1,−3,3,−1) sum to zero. If it first enters the second triangle, its coefficient is −3 +3 −1 = −1−3+3−1=−1; entry in the third gives 3 −1 =23−1=2, and entry in the fourth gives −1−1. Thus a finite difference depends both on which triangles contain the point and on changes of its weight. We separate these two effects below. Avoiding floor crossings controls the weights, but does not remove the newly added strips.

It does not exclude a different fixed operator, different shifts, a boundary correction or a sparse-defect statement restricted to a suitable infinite subsequence.

What the Hecke–Mahler comparison does and does not supply.

In the published Luca–Ouaknine–Worrell article [26], the same fixed integer coefficients are applied to shifts of one integer sequence. The resulting nonzero terms must have expanding gaps and uniform polynomial variation; the original sequence must also have polynomial growth. Theorem 6 then gives a fixed-base value criterion. Theorem 8 verifies that condition for 𝑓(⌊𝑚𝜗 +𝜌⌋)f(⌊mϑ+ρ⌋) when 𝑓 ∈ℤ[𝑥]f∈Z[x] is nonconstant, 𝜗,𝜌 ∈(0,1)ϑ,ρ∈(0,1) and 𝜗ϑ is irrational. These interval restrictions belong to that normalised combinatorial statement. Their main value theorem, Theorem 1, allows every real 𝜌ρ and every irrational real 𝜗ϑ, with any algebraic base 𝛽β satisfying |𝛽| >1|β|>1. Claim 10 uses a finite difference of order deg⁡𝑓 +1deg⁡f+1, which vanishes when no floor crossing occurs. This is a polynomial evaluated at a floor, not merely an integer sequence of polynomial growth. Our 𝑚𝑎ma is instead a weighted lattice count. Proposition 12.2 separates floor crossings from its moving boundary, and Example 12.3 shows that the latter can survive a cubic difference even with no crossings.

There is a second distinction. In our displayed shift identity the coefficient of 𝑚𝑎+𝑗𝑟ma+jr is 15𝑐𝑗𝛾𝑎,𝑗𝑟15cjγa,jr, which can depend on 𝑎a. For example, 𝑃1 =2P1=2, 𝑃2 =12P2=12 and 𝑃3 =120P3=120 give 𝛾0,1 =1/3γ0,1=1/3 but 𝛾1,1 =1/5γ1,1=1/5. These factors are required by the denominator chain. A support estimate for 𝐷𝑟,𝑎Dr,a is therefore not by itself a verification of Definition 5 for the sequence (𝑚𝑎)(ma). No fixed-coefficient representation to which that theorem applies has been established here.

For a variable-denominator analogue, a useful hypothesis would be a fixed choice of coefficients and shifts 𝑟𝑛 →∞rn→∞ for which Δ𝑛 ={𝑎 ≥0 :𝐷𝑟𝑛,𝑎 ≠0}Δn={a≥0:Drn,a≠0} is infinite and distinct members are at least 𝜂𝑟𝑛ηrn apart, for a fixed 𝜂 >0η>0. Even this would leave the uniform polynomial-variation requirement, for example

|𝐷𝑟𝑛,𝑎′|≤𝐶((𝑎′−𝑎)𝑑+|𝐷𝑟𝑛,𝑎|)(𝑎<𝑎′, 𝑎,𝑎′∈Δ𝑛),|Drn,a′|≤C((a′−a)d+|Drn,a|)(a<a′, a,a′∈Δn),

with 𝐶,𝑑C,d independent of 𝑛n, 𝑎a and 𝑎′a′. This is a condition on the gaps between nonzero terms, not merely on their density: even a set of density zero can contain adjacent pairs. It also requires infinitely many nonzero terms for each selected shift. A small but nonzero term at every index would fail it, and an identically zero difference would also fail the infinitude requirement. The cited paper constructs suitable shifts for the polynomial-floor sequences just described; no such result is proved for our weighted counts. The bound 𝑂((𝑎 +𝑟 +1)2)O((a+r+1)2) controls absolute size: it depends on the location 𝑎a itself. The variation condition instead bounds a later nonzero term by the gap from an earlier one and the size of that earlier term, with constants uniform in the shift. The absolute-size bound alone gives no such comparison. The denominator chain itself is not a fixed-base power sequence. The next proposition shows what is lost in two direct fixed-base recodings. A value criterion for the original chain would need a separate proof, including non-cancellation and the Diophantine height estimates required by a Subspace-Theorem argument. These heights measure the numerators and denominators of the approximating algebraic quantities; they are unrelated to the running LCM HH. The finite set of prime divisors alone does not provide those estimates.

Why a finite alphabet of bases is not enough.

Kebis, Luca, Ouaknine, Scoones and Worrell [27] work with fixed-base series whose coefficients lie in a finite algebraic alphabet. Their echoing condition requires long near-repetitions, separated intervals containing the mismatches, and nonzero weighted mismatch sums on at least two of those intervals. Claim 7 supplies the non-cancellation step in the proof of the value theorem. Merely having finitely many letters does not give these properties. The four-letter radix sequence is not the numerator sequence: the actual 𝑚𝑎ma is unbounded. A recoding would have to preserve the scalar value, identify its coefficient alphabet and verify the echoing conditions. No fixed-base recoding with verified echoing properties is proved here.

Two natural bases expose the tradeoff. The least integer base whose powers clear every 𝑃𝑛Pn is 3030, while base 88 matches the growth of 𝑃𝑛 =H⁡(2𝑛)Pn=H⁡(2n). The former keeps integrality; the latter keeps polynomial size.

A rational number need not have eventually periodic digits when the radices vary. For example, take radix 55 at the indices 1,2,4,8,…1,2,4,8,… and radix 33 elsewhere. The constant tail fraction 1/21/2 gives digit 22 at those indices and 11 elsewhere. These digits are not eventually periodic, but their mixed-radix expansion sums to 1/21/2. This example uses different radices from our four possible bases; it shows why fixed-base eventual periodicity cannot be transferred to a variable-radix expansion. Our digits also depend on the actual tail fractions, not just on the four-letter radix sequence. The construction supplies neither a fixed-base expansion with verified echoing properties nor a bound on its digit complexity.

Adamczewski–Bugeaud’s complexity theorem [30] concerns the actual digits of an integer-base expansion: for an algebraic irrational their length-𝑛n block complexity divided by 𝑛n tends to infinity. Neither (𝑏𝑎)(ba) nor the uncarried (𝑒𝑎)(ea) is such a digit expansion of 𝛼α.

The tail formulation requires that no positive integer multiplier coprime to 3030 make any 𝑋𝑎Xa, 𝑎 ≥1a≥1, integral. Function-theoretic representations

The elementary proof of irrationality of D{2,3,5}D{2,3,5} gives no transcendence conclusion. Recall that

D{2,3,5}=1+∑𝑡∈{2𝑛,3𝑛,5𝑛:𝑛≥1}12⌊log2⁡𝑡⌋3⌊log3⁡𝑡⌋5⌊log5⁡𝑡⌋.D{2,3,5}=1+∑t∈{2n,3n,5n:n≥1}12⌊log2⁡t⌋3⌊log3⁡t⌋5⌊log5⁡t⌋.

Each running LCM is counted once at its first jump, unlike the repeated sum. The bases in (14) come from these same jumps. For two primes a representation by one Hecke–Mahler value proves transcendence (Section 4). A corresponding three-prime representation has not been constructed here.

Problem 12.7 (an exact function representing the distinct-height sum). Transcendence of D{2,3,5}D{2,3,5} is not proved here. For a functional approach to it, first specify the function, its coefficient field and convergence domain, then prove an exact identity for D{2,3,5}D{2,3,5}, and only then apply a stated value theorem. A conditional theorem must display the extra nondegeneracy assumption; a no-representation theorem must specify the class it excludes.

For (𝑝,𝑞,𝑟) =(2,3,5)(p,q,r)=(2,3,5), the two slopes in the rank proof are log5⁡2 =𝜃5log5⁡2=θ5 and log5⁡3 =𝜃5/𝜃3log5⁡3=θ5/θ3, not 𝜃3θ3 and 𝜃5θ5. Each is irrational: a rational value would equate a positive power of 55 with a positive power of 22 or 33. The proof chooses the row and column indices independently. It therefore needs no rational independence of 1,𝜃3,𝜃51,θ3,θ5 and no density assertion for the singly indexed orbit ({𝑛𝜃3},{𝑛𝜃5})({nθ3},{nθ5}). Any functional approach that needs such a stronger hypothesis must establish it separately.

A finite-dimensional encoding must preserve equality of the functions it is meant to represent. If two encodings agree but their functions do not, the encoding cannot justify a conclusion about those functions. The Lean sources express this condition as a factorisation through a finite-dimensional space and prove that the resulting space of functions is then finite-dimensional (identity for the carry, map to functions, finite-dimensional conclusion). They also bound the carry residue and its digit in their stated intervals (residue bound, digit bound). These conditional linear-algebra statements neither construct a function representing D{2,3,5}D{2,3,5} nor show that a corresponding function space must be infinite-dimensional.

The cited value theorems and their hypotheses.

Pellarin’s rank-one theorem concerns quadratic irrational slopes and algebraic evaluation points in the convergence domain [31]. The prime-logarithm slopes used here are not quadratic: each log𝑟⁡𝑝logr⁡p is irrational by unique factorisation, and the Gelfond–Schneider theorem then makes it transcendental, since 𝑟log𝑟⁡𝑝 =𝑝rlogr⁡p=p is algebraic.1 This rules out direct substitution of those slopes into Pellarin’s quadratic-slope theorem. It does not rule out a different representation of the scalar sum, and it does not affect the two-prime argument above, which uses a theorem for general irrational slopes.

In Pellarin’s reduced-slope normalisation, the rank-one condition says that the evaluation points arise from a common point by the quadratic order’s monomial action, up to multiplication by torsion points. For a single evaluation point it is automatic: use that point itself and the identity action. For several points it is a condition to check, not a consequence of having two lattice coordinates. Under it, algebraic independence of the values is equivalent to ℚQ-linear independence of the specified auxiliary formal Laurent series; the rank-one condition alone does not imply independence. This module rank is not the rank of our reciprocal kernel. No exact representation suitable for this theorem has been constructed here, but infinite kernel rank alone does not preclude one.

For one variable, Adamczewski and Faverjon’s proofs of Nishioka’s theorem and the lifting theorem are regular-point results [32]. Regularity means that the system matrix stays defined and invertible along the evaluation orbit. Their multivariate lifting theorem [33] additionally assumes an admissible transformation–point pair. Its growth, decay and nonvanishing conditions are specified in Definition 5.1; none follows merely from writing a double sum. Lifting transfers a relation among values to one among functions; a transcendence application must exclude the latter. A Mahler system alone cannot do this, as the constant function 11 illustrates.

Regularity of a preselected system is not, however, a universal prerequisite for Mahler’s method. The same paper’s Theorem 1.1 treats univariate Mahler functions at algebraic points in the punctured unit disc where their values are defined, without that regularity hypothesis. The hypotheses must therefore be matched to the particular theorem being invoked. No exact Mahler representation or suitable evaluation data for this sum over distinct running LCMs are constructed here. The locators for this paper refer to its 68-page author manuscript, not the older 52-page arXiv version.

Hypotheses for auxiliary integer recurrences

For ordered primes 𝑝1 <⋯ <𝑝𝑠p1<⋯<ps, the interval (𝑝𝑎1,𝑝𝑎+11)(p1a,p1a+1) contains at most one power of each 𝑝𝑖 >𝑝1pi>p1. The radix including the final 𝑝1p1-jump consequently belongs to

{𝑝1𝑠∏𝑖=2𝑝𝜀𝑖𝑖:𝜀𝑖∈{0,1}}.{p1∏i=2spiεi:εi∈{0,1}}.

This finite alphabet determines neither the frequency of the radices nor the error terms in the weighted block counts. Estimates for those quantities, or for specified shifted kernels, would be additional arithmetic inputs. The conditional statements about integer recurrences below keep such inputs explicit.

Some auxiliary results explain why bounded integer approximations alone are insufficient. Here are their hypotheses in explicit form.

Let 𝑗(𝑛) ∈{2,3,5}j(n)∈{2,3,5} label a sequence of jumps, and suppose each label occurs. A perturbation 𝜀𝑛εn in an additive abelian group has sum zero on every interval [𝑎,𝑏)[a,b) whose endpoints have the same label exactly when

for three potential values 𝑢(2),𝑢(3),𝑢(5)u(2),u(3),u(5). One direction follows by telescoping. Conversely, the zero-sum assumption makes ∑𝑘<𝑛𝜀𝑘∑k<nεk the same at any two indices with the same label. Assign that common value to 𝑢(𝑗(𝑛))u(j(n)); every label occurs, so all three values are defined. Consecutive partial sums then give the displayed identity. In the usual terminology, the perturbation is a coboundary of the function 𝑢u on the labels: it is the difference of successive potential values. This is a telescoping condition, not a bound on the size of the perturbation. It does not by itself force the perturbation to vanish: unequal potential values give nonzero differences when the label changes. If the perturbation also vanishes on a genuine 2 →32→3 transition and on a genuine 2 →52→5 transition, all three potential values agree, so every perturbation is zero.

For an integer sequence satisfying 𝑐𝑛+1 =𝑏𝑛𝑐𝑛 −𝐷𝑚𝑛cn+1=bncn−Dmn, compare it with an integer sequence 𝑧𝑛zn. Define the error 𝑒𝑛 =𝐷𝑧𝑛 −𝑐𝑛en=Dzn−cn and the perturbation 𝜀𝑛 =𝑏𝑛𝑧𝑛 −𝑧𝑛+1 −𝑚𝑛εn=bnzn−zn+1−mn. Then

𝑒𝑛+1=𝑏𝑛𝑒𝑛−𝐷𝜀𝑛.en+1=bnen−Dεn.

This contradicts even one bound |𝑒𝑁| <2𝑁|eN|<2N, and therefore also excludes a uniform bound for all 𝑁N. The nonzero initial error is essential: the identically zero error causes no contradiction.

A calculation at four consecutive indices gives a related obstruction. If 0 <𝑇𝑖 <10<Ti<1, 𝑧𝑖 ∈ℤzi∈Z and |𝑧𝑖 −𝑇𝑖| <1|zi−Ti|<1, then 𝑧𝑖zi is 00 or 11. For bases 2,3,2,52,3,2,5, the equalities 2𝑧0 −𝑧1 −1 =02z0−z1−1=0 and 2𝑧2 −𝑧3 −1 =02z2−z3−1=0 force all four integers to be 11. The sum of the first two perturbations is then

not zero. Thus unit accuracy, the two exact equalities and a zero sum on that block cannot all hold. Unit accuracy alone does not give either exact equality.

No integer approximation to the tails of 𝑆S is constructed here that satisfies all these conditions. Rationality supplies integer carries of at most quadratic growth, but not the additional zero-sum and transition identities. The carries obtained from 𝑆S satisfy a weighted block identity instead. Applying the auxiliary results would require that identity to imply their hypotheses, or would require a different construction of the integer approximations.

There is also a conditional criterion for a sum supported on the powers of 22. Its elementary ingredients can be stated without introducing another formal vocabulary. From 𝑦′ =𝑏𝑦 −1y′=by−1 with 𝑏 >0b>0 and 0 <𝑦′ <10<y′<1 one gets 1/𝑏 <𝑦 <2/𝑏1/b<y<2/b. For integers 𝑎 >0a>0 and 𝑝 ≥3p≥3, if 𝑢 >1/𝑎u>1/a and 𝑣 <2/(𝑝𝑎)v<2/(pa), then 𝑢 −𝑣 >1/(3𝑎)u−v>1/(3a). Finally, a real number 𝑥x is irrational if, for every positive integer 𝑑d, there are integers 𝑛,𝑘n,k with 0 <|𝑛𝑥 −𝑘| <1/𝑑0<|nx−k|<1/d.

To use these observations for a series, the conditional result requires exact identities 𝑦𝑀 =𝐻𝑀𝑥 −𝑧𝑀yM=HMx−zM, with 𝐻𝑀,𝑧𝑀 ∈ℤHM,zM∈Z, and, for every positive 𝑑d, two indices with different 𝐻𝑀HM, different 𝑦𝑀yM, and |𝑦𝑀 −𝑦𝑀′| <1/𝑑|yM−yM′|<1/d. Their difference gives the required nonzero linear form. Equal tail values would give zero and would not suffice; a merely bounded gap would not suffice either. Indeed, for a rational 𝑥x of denominator 𝑑d, every nonzero difference of this form has size at least 1/𝑑1/d. No concrete series in this record is shown to satisfy all these clearing and arbitrarily small nonzero-gap conditions.

The unresolved repeated-sum question

Theorem 1.1 settles the sum over distinct running LCMs for {2,3,5}{2,3,5}. The ordinary arguments in Remarks 5.1 and 5.10 treat all finite prime supports and the prime-power subseries, respectively, pending formalisation. Remark 5.8 records the finite-state calculations; the collision in the admissible automaton language for {2,3,5,7}{2,3,5,7} limits that interval criterion only. For R{2,3,5}R{2,3,5} we have the exact coefficients and recurrence, quadratic tail bounds and denominator-clearing formula. The remaining question is whether all eventual integral reduced tails can be excluded. Equivalently, the required residue segments must exist for every admissible 𝐵B beyond every prescribed starting index. The fixed-start formula explains the necessity of these quantifiers, and the strip identity shows why a no-crossing argument alone does not prove the required cancellation.

The rank and uniform-norm results concern the kernel, not the arithmetic of its sum. Finite tests, countability, radix recoding and denominator support do not close the remaining argument. The settled two-prime case uses Fan’s earlier reduction to the cited Hecke–Mahler value theorem.

Verification and reproducibility

Proof sources.

The evidence record fixes the source versions and individual statement associations. These are earlier checks; this revision makes no fresh formal-verification claim.

The general distinct-value assertion and its four word-and-torus arguments are stated as remarks with complete ordinary proofs in Section 5.1; they have no Lean proofs. The source record reports that the general and prime-power subseries arguments were found on 26 September 2026 and checked by a second AI agent, whose corrections were incorporated. It records no human review; the present revision does not constitute a new independent review. No separate literature search for the prime-power subseries theorem at |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3 is recorded, and no priority claim is made for it. The subseries identities also have ordinary proofs. The program two_tail.py checks their finite instances in exact arithmetic.

For {2,3,5}{2,3,5} the separate theorem for the sum over distinct values has a Lean proof; its source record says that Comparator had not been run on it. The general affine-block calculation, decoding criterion and finite-set application are also remarks with ordinary proofs; the last additionally uses exact computation. Their formal coverage is restricted to the {2,3,5}{2,3,5} case with one block and the interval of Section 2. The linear-flow and Smith-factor results likewise have the ordinary proofs printed here; no additional formal coverage is inferred for them.

The two-prime deduction is credited to Fan [17]. Its formal proof assumes the cited Hecke–Mahler value theorem, as specified in Section 14; its algebraic identities are unconditional. The weighted-triangle and shift identities, denominator formula, scaled dichotomy, uniqueness argument, residue limit, strip decomposition and recoding also have written proofs here. Their individual formal associations are retained, without a blanket assertion that every result in the record is formalised. Kernel acceptance uses the standard axioms allowed by the linked checks and is not an independent review of the paper-to-statement correspondence.

The twelve-block enclosure, denominator bound and eight mixed-radix digits have finite exact proofs. The two large exclusions have saved witnesses and exact checkers, and the larger scan has a saved run. None of these finite computations proves the residue inequalities beyond every starting index. No Comparator replay is claimed for the general or subseries arguments.

Artefact and data availability.

The links in the source inventory and to the integer-arithmetic checker open a fixed revision of the repository. The witnesses and exact checkers for the two large numerical exclusions and the saved larger scan are in the large-computation directory. The programs for sums over distinct values recompute the constants of Theorem 1.1 and the certificates of Remark 5.8 in exact rational arithmetic, with two independent computations of the tail intervals, and store their outputs; a fast test checks them against the stored outputs. The same directory checks the finite illustrations of Section 5.1 and the block identity for {2,3,5,7}{2,3,5,7}.

Further examples, conditional lemmas and source references

We collect the historical statements and then separate the lemmas on integer recurrences from their three-prime application. Their explicit divisibility and segment hypotheses specify what another recurrence must supply. Finite examples and the declaration inventory complete the record.

The historical and catalogue record

For a singleton 𝑃 ={𝑝}P={p}, we have 𝑎𝑛 =𝑝𝑛−1an=pn−1 and [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛] =𝑝𝑛−1[a1,…,an]=pn−1, so both sums equal 𝑝/(𝑝 −1)p/(p−1). Erdős’s 1988 account calls the infinite-prime case a simple exercise and presents irrationality for a finite number of primes greater than one as a probable extension [2]. Bloom’s catalogue records an open problem at the access date of 28 July 2026 [4]. These are dated source statements, not a fresh determination of the catalogue’s present status.

In the letter written on 1 January 1973 and published in 1974, Erdős calls the irrationality of R𝑃RP a conjecture that he cannot prove, and says that he can show the sum over the distinct values of [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑘][a1,…,ak] to be irrational [3]. That sum is D𝑃DP. The letter introduces its primes as 𝑝1,…,𝑝𝑠p1,…,ps, later writing 𝑝𝑟pr, without restricting their number, so the singleton calculation forces the qualification |𝑃| ≥2|P|≥2. It prints no argument. The catalogue has cited the letter for Problem #269 since 28 December 2025, after the letter was quoted in the site’s discussion of missing problems [5], and its page records Erdős’s statement about the distinct values. The catalogue page says that Erdős proved the statement; the letter asserts it and prints no argument. Remark 5.1 proves it for every finite 𝑃P with |𝑃| ≥2|P|≥2. For |𝑃| =2|P|=2 it was already a consequence of the Hecke–Mahler transcendence theorem of Loxton and van der Poorten [16] and Bugeaud and Laurent [15], through the affine identity of Section 4, by the route Fan used for R{𝑝,𝑞}R{p,q}. We do not know what argument Erdős had in mind.

We have not found a proof of the assertion in print. Erdős and Graham state only the question for R𝑃RP: the sum is irrational for infinite 𝑃P, and they ask what happens for finite 𝑃P with more than one element [1]; the sum over distinct running LCMs does not appear there. Erdős’s survey of 1975 on the irrationality of series [8] does not mention the running least common multiple of the 𝑃P-smooth integers, his survey of 1980 on combinatorial number theory [6] does not discuss irrationality, and his survey of 1988 states only the question for R𝑃RP [2]. Every Hecke–Mahler transcendence theorem we found, including those of Loxton and van der Poorten, Bugeaud and Laurent, and Luca–Ouaknine–Worrell [26], has a single slope, and so reaches D𝑃DP only for |𝑃| =2|P|=2. The rationality criterion of Diananda and Oppenheim [7], which condenses a Cantor series into blocks of consecutive terms, has the form of the dyadic argument of Section 2; it restates rationality and does not decide D𝑃DP. The discussion thread of Problem #269 contains no argument for D𝑃DP with |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3, and the Formal Conjectures statement [9] concerns R𝑃RP only. The Cantor-series criteria of Erdős–Straus [18] and Hančl–Tijdeman [19] do not apply to D𝑃DP, as explained in Section 2. The search did not reach the sections on irrational series in Guy’s Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, or MathSciNet reviews. The unresolved target of this record is the repeated series R𝑃RP; a transcendence statement for D𝑃DP with |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3 is a separate question (Problem 12.7).

On 26 June 2026 Steve Fan posted the two-prime factorisation, the Hecke–Mahler reduction and the transcendence conclusion in the discussion thread of the problem’s page [17]; the comment itself notes that the argument does not seem to generalise immediately to |𝑃| ≥3|P|≥3, and a reply there observes that it applies to arbitrary coprime pairs. The first public version of this note is dated 22 July 2026, after Fan’s post. We retain the calculation as exposition and make no priority claim for it.

The statement of the problem has been formalised as a conjecture with an unfilled proof in the Formal Conjectures collection [9]. In the cited source, the rational, irrational and infinite-prime assertions end in sorry. Its Nat-indexed series includes the empty-prefix least-common-multiple term, so its value differs from the conventional one by a rational constant; transporting a theorem across that boundary needs an explicit series-identification lemma, which is not supplied here.

Integer recurrences in their general form

Consider an arbitrary integer recurrence with positive integer radices. Divisibility and the existence of segments satisfying the residue inequality must now be supplied as hypotheses. For the actual three-prime radices, the criterion below shows that each integer solution is eventually divisible by the smooth part of a denominator. It still leaves the residue-inequality hypothesis to be proved. The comparison with Cantor-series criteria is in Section 9.

Let 𝐷D and 𝐵B be positive integers with 𝐷 =𝐷sm𝐵D=DsmB, where 𝐷sm =2𝑢3𝑣5𝑤Dsm=2u3v5w, 𝑢,𝑣,𝑤 ∈ℕu,v,w∈N and gcd(𝐵,30) =1gcd(B,30)=1. Let (𝑐𝑛)(cn) be an integer sequence satisfying 𝑐𝑛+1 =𝑏𝑛𝑐𝑛 −𝐷𝑚𝑛cn+1=bncn−Dmn for integer sequences (𝑏𝑛)(bn) and (𝑚𝑛)(mn). For these general sequences, form 𝑊W and 𝐹F by the recursions in Section 10; a segment satisfying the residue inequality must have 𝑊 ≠0W≠0, and its modulus is |𝑊||W|. In the factorisation below the quotients 𝑑𝑛dn are required to be integers; writing 𝑐𝑛 =𝐷sm𝑑𝑛cn=Dsmdn asserts divisibility, not just an identity in ℚQ.

Proposition 13.2 (segments satisfying the residue inequality exclude a positive bounded integer solution). Let (𝑏𝑛)(bn) and (𝑚𝑛)(mn) be sequences of nonnegative integers, let 𝐺 :ℕ>0 ×ℕ →ℕG:N>0×N→N, and assume the residue condition (20) for these sequences and 𝐺G, using |𝑊ℓ,ℎ| >0|Wℓ,h|>0 as the modulus. Fix 𝐵 >0B>0 coprime to 3030. There is no integral sequence (𝑑𝑛)(dn) satisfying simultaneously 𝑑𝑛+1 =𝑏𝑛𝑑𝑛 −𝐵𝑚𝑛dn+1=bndn−Bmn, 𝑑𝑛 >0dn>0 and |𝑑𝑛| ≤𝐺(𝐵,𝑛)|dn|≤G(B,n) for every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0.

Proof. Choose one segment satisfying the residue inequality (ℓ,ℎ)(ℓ,h). The iterated recurrence gives 𝑑ℓ+ℎ ≡ −𝐵𝐹ℓ,ℎdℓ+h≡−BFℓ,h modulo |𝑊ℓ,ℎ||Wℓ,h|. The endpoint value is positive and at most 𝐺(𝐵,ℓ +ℎ)G(B,ℓ+h), whereas the least positive residue of the right-hand side exceeds that bound, so Proposition 10.1 applies. ◻

The residue-inequality hypothesis is the substantial arithmetic assumption. It requires a residue above the bound, not just a rapidly growing product of bases. For example, the constant data 𝑏𝑛 =2bn=2, 𝑚𝑛 =1mn=1 have the positive solution 𝑑𝑛 =𝐵dn=B. For any bound 𝐺(𝐵,𝑛) ≥𝐵G(B,n)≥B, every segment has 𝑊 =2ℎW=2h, 𝐹 =2ℎ −1F=2h−1 and least positive residue at most 𝐵B, so the hypothesis fails. For the actual three-prime coefficients and 𝐺 =𝐾G=K, Theorem 10.2 makes the residue-inequality hypothesis equivalent to irrationality of 𝑆S. That equivalence does not hold for an arbitrary choice of 𝐺G.

Coprimality with 3030 selects the denominators covered by the hypothesis; once a segment is fixed, the finite contradiction does not use it. The conventions cover the edge cases: a zero product of the bases is excluded, a zero residue is represented by the full modulus, and positivity prevents the endpoint value from vanishing. The version stated with a nonzero smooth factor assumes the exact factorisation 𝑐𝑛 =𝐷sm𝑑𝑛cn=Dsmdn, the corresponding recurrence for (𝑐𝑛)(cn) and the positive upper bound for (𝑑𝑛)(dn), and gives the same contradiction.

Even retaining the actual radix sequence and quadratic growth does not force irrationality if the numerators are changed. For the same 𝑏𝑎ba, prescribe the positive integer carries (𝑎 +3)2(a+3)2 and set

ˆ𝑚𝑎=𝑏𝑎(𝑎+3)2−(𝑎+4)2.m^a=ba(a+3)2−(a+4)2.

Both these integer coefficients and the prescribed carries have quadratic order, because 2 ≤𝑏𝑎 ≤302≤ba≤30. Nevertheless, finite telescoping gives

𝑁−1∑𝑎=0ˆ𝑚𝑎𝑃𝑎+1=9−(𝑁+3)2𝑃𝑁⟶9.∑a=0N−1m^aPa+1=9−(N+3)2PN⟶9.

This example keeps the exact radices, not the actual block multiplicities or their numerical upper bound 𝑄Q. It shows why the arithmetic of the specific 𝑚𝑎ma, rather than the radix alphabet and growth orders alone, must enter a proof for 𝑆S.

Dependencies and remaining questions

The table separates the established special cases from the ordinary generalisations awaiting formalisation and the unresolved repeated-sum condition. Exact kernel rank concerns separation of a function; the residue criterion concerns a scalar sum and still needs arithmetic existence for its segments.

Result Dependency and limit
Running LCMs and intervals of constancy Prime-power divisibility and unique factorisation. Their geometry alone gives no irrationality statement.
Two-prime values Earlier factorisation plus the cited external Hecke–Mahler value theorem. The reduction to that theorem is checked in Lean; the theorem itself is a cited input (Section 14).
Distinct values, every 𝑃P Integrality of the scaled tails, rearranged chains at a return of the logarithmic flow, Kronecker’s theorem and an Euler characteristic count on a two-dimensional subtorus. Ordinary proof checked by a second agent; no Lean proof. It stops for the repeated sums because their scaled tails are unbounded.
Prime-power subseries The same two-tail comparison with the integer 𝑓𝑝fp and a chain chosen near the origin of the torus; no two-wall lemma. Ordinary proof checked by a second agent; no Lean proof. Says nothing about the whole repeated sum.
Distinct values, blocks Dyadic blocks, finitely many affine maps with disjoint images, integrality of the scaled tails and the irrationality of log⁡𝑝/log⁡𝑞log⁡p/log⁡q. The theorem for {2,3,5}{2,3,5} is checked in Lean; the general criterion has an ordinary proof, and Remark 5.8 adds exact finite computations. No statement about the repeated sums.
Arbitrary-order rank Diagonal rescaling, separate one-dimensional densities and a staircase determinant; checked in Lean.
Tail recurrence Counting the original multiplicities, normalising by half the boundary running LCM, and convergence; an abstract recurrence would not identify the sum.
Denominator reduction A finite prefix with cleared denominators and an upper bound for positive integer tails. The first valid index is determined exactly (Proposition 9.4); checked in Lean.
Residue criterion The actual recurrence, a dominating bound and segment products comparable to 8ℎ8h; the inequality at arbitrarily late starts remains unproved.
Weighted differences Exact reindexing and the contributions of the new boundary strips; integer enumeration checks the displayed counterexample to third-difference cancellation.
Finite computations Direct checks settle only their individual segments. The two large exclusions have published witnesses and exact checkers, and the larger scan a published saved run; none is a theorem input.

None of these results proves irrationality of the repeated sum R𝑃RP for three or more primes.

The formal two-prime reduction

The source note in Section 12.5 distinguishes ordinary proofs from individual formal associations. For Theorem 1.2, the Lean development verifies the reduction of that theorem to the transcendence of the Hecke–Mahler boundary sum at an irrational 𝜃 ∈(0,1)θ∈(0,1) and nonzero algebraic 𝛽,𝛼β,α with |𝛽| <1|β|<1 and |𝛽||𝛼|𝜃 <1|β||α|θ<1, which is Theorem 1.1 of Bugeaud and Laurent [15] in the case 𝜌 =0ρ=0, due to Loxton and van der Poorten [16]. Lean does not prove that input; the Lean theorem assumes it. The formal development checks the following parts of the reduction: the running least-common-multiple identity, the selection of the single power of 𝑞q between consecutive powers of 𝑝p, the factorisation of the repeated sum, the identification of the distinct running values, the telescoping identity, the boundary identity (6) expressing 𝐴A through the Hecke–Mahler sum, the irrationality of log⁡𝑝/log⁡𝑞log⁡p/log⁡q, and each side condition verified before the value theorem is applied. The two identities expressing D{𝑝,𝑞}D{p,q} and R{𝑝,𝑞}R{p,q} as polynomials in 𝐴A are unconditional and carry no additional input.

A theorem whose own statement is conditional is formalised exactly as stated. Theorem 1.2 is asserted unconditionally in this record, and its Lean counterpart carries the additional named input described here.
